title: Implications of Full-System Modeling for Superconducting Architectures
problem: As Moore's Law slows, alternative computing substrates like superconducting electronics are being explored for ultra-low power and high-speed computation. However, their architectural implications for full systems remain unclear, particularly regarding cache bandwidth, interconnect design, and memory bottlenecks.
motivation: Superconducting electronics offer 100x+ clock frequency advantages, but the value to realistic workloads remains unquantified. Full-system modeling is needed to understand where superconducting benefits compound with memory hierarchies and interconnects.
method: First full-system superconducting architecture simulation in gem5, including superconducting cores (100 GHz) and cryogenic semiconductor cores (4 GHz), multilevel caches, RISC-V ISA, and integration with SRNoC superconducting interconnect and NOVA graph accelerator. Evaluation on SPEC CPU2006 and compute-intensive benchmarks.
key_novelty: First comprehensive system-level modeling of superconducting cores and caches with realistic interconnects and memory systems in a widely-used simulator.
contributions: gem5 extension with 100 GHz superconducting RISC-V cores and 4 GHz cryogenic cores
Multilevel cache hierarchy design for superconducting systems
Integration of SRNoC superconducting interconnect in full-system context
Demonstration that superconducting benefits are workload and data-width dependent
Identification of 800 GB/s cache bandwidth requirement as critical design challenge
limitations: Room-temperature DRAM remains a bottleneck; SRNoC interconnect highly sensitive to data width. Superconducting technology appears better suited for domain-specific accelerators than general-purpose CPUs.
